newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, orange juice prices soar on supply worry.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, orange juice prices soar on supply worry.

text.p: Coffee prices kept a six-week rally going Monday by setting life-of-contract highs, and frozen concentrate orange juice futures soared after a weekend freeze in Florida damaged citrus crops.
Those gains, and strength in copper prices, helped push the Knight Ridder Commodity Research Bureau index of 17 futures contracts up 0.35 point to close at 241.98 points.

At New York's Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for March delivery closed up 5.25 cents a pound at 129.25 cents. Contract highs were set in the March and May deliveries, with March up 25 percent from its close of 103.25 cents on Dec. 6.
Supply worries have fed the coffee price surge, with news from Colombia and Brazil on Monday only feeding more buying by speculators.

In Brazil, the top coffee exporter, the head of the primary commodities department at the Industry and Commerce Ministry said Brazil's 1997/98 coffee crop may come in between 18 million and 20 million 132-pound bags, compared with government estimates of 25 million bags for the previous season.

In Colombia, the No. 2 exporter, a strike by dockworkers at the port of Buenaventura entered its sixth day Monday. The strike has blocked shipment of about 160,000 bags of coffee from the port, which handles about 60 percent of the country's coffee exports.

"This was the quarter supplies were supposed to come in and alleviate the tightness," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "With the Colombian situation and the Brazilian estimates, it does not look like that is happening."

At the New York Cotton Exchange, orange juice futures also soared after temperatures in Florida dipped as low as 19 degrees over the weekend and caused ice to form in some fruit still awaiting harvest. March orange juice closed up 5.95 cents a pound at 85.85 cents.
"We are going to see some damage, especially in the specialty fruit varieties remaining on trees," said Bobby McKown, head of citrus growers group Florida Citrus Mutual.
Citrus can be damaged when temperatures fall below 27 degrees for at least four hours. As of Jan. 12, about 67 percent of Florida's citrus crop remained on trees.
The Agriculture Department has already estimated this year's Florida's orange crop at a record 220 million 90-pound boxes.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange's Comex division, copper prices rose to their highest levels since the Sumitomo trading scandal erupted last June. March copper ended 1.70 cents higher at 107.55 cents a pound.

William O'Neill of Merrill Lynch said copper stockpiles at the London Metal Exchange were expected to rise 2,000 to 5,000 metric tons in weekly data expected Tuesday. But indications pointed to good physical demand early this year.
"The market has been expecting a little bit of a stock increase for a while, and then as we move into February we will start to see a decline," O'Neill said.
Good performances in other base metals, particularly zinc, nickel and even lead and aluminum, were also helping copper consolidate and make gains, O'Neill added.

Oil prices closed lower, with milder temperatures forecast for the "heating oil belt" of the Northeast this week and ample supplies fueling selling. February heating oil at the Nymex ended at 66.94 cents a gallon, down 1.50 cents.
"We have weather services calling for several days of warming when refiners are now pretty well positioned with supplies," said Jeff Foose, trader with KCS Energy Inc.
February crude ended 18 cents lower at $25.23 a barrel and February gasoline 0.86 cent a gallon lower at 67.23 cents.
